concepts: Reciprocal-type equations: substitution $x+\frac1x=t$ and its range
questions.question: The number of real solutions of the equation $3\left(x^2+\frac1{x^2}\right)-2\left(x+\frac1x\right)+5=0$ is:
questions.key_idea: For real $x$, $\left|x+\frac1x\right|\ge2$, so a root $t$ with $|t|<2$ gives no real $x$.
solution: Both values lie in $(-2,2)$, outside the allowed set $(-\infty,-2]\cup[2,\infty)$.
Hence no real $x$ exists: the number of real solutions is $0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Complete the square in $x$ and in $\frac1x$ separately to show the left side is always positive.
solution: Each square is $\ge0$, so the expression is at least $\frac{13}3>0$ for every real $x\ne0$.
Hence there is no real solution: $0$ solutions (check: at $x=1$ both forms give $7$).

useful_results: For real $x\ne0$: $\left|x+\frac1x\right|\ge2$ (AM-GM), with equality only at $x=\pm1$; so $t=x+\frac1x$ never takes a value in $(-2,2)$.
Reciprocal (palindromic) equation of degree $2n$: divide by $x^n$ and put $t=x+\frac1x$; each root $t$ with $|t|<2$ gives a pair of non-real roots of modulus 1.
Here $t=1$ and $t=-\frac13$ give four non-real roots (for $t=1$: $x=e^{\pm i\pi/3}$).

concepts: Common root of two quadratics and relations between roots and coefficients
questions.question: Let $\lambda\ne0$ be a real number. Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of $14x^2-31x+3\lambda=0$ and $\alpha,\gamma$ be the roots of $35x^2-53x+4\lambda=0$. Then $\frac{3\alpha}\beta$ and $\frac{4\alpha}\gamma$ are the roots of the equation:
questions.key_idea: The shared root $\alpha$ satisfies both equations; eliminating $\lambda$ fixes $\alpha$.
solution: $\alpha$ is a root of both: $14\alpha^2-31\alpha+3\lambda=0$ ...(i) and $35\alpha^2-53\alpha+4\lambda=0$ ...(ii).
So $\alpha=0$ or $\alpha=\frac57$. $\alpha=0$ would give $\lambda=0$, which is not allowed; hence $\alpha=\frac57$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Express the new roots through $\alpha^2/\lambda$ using the products $\alpha\beta,\alpha\gamma$, then solve a small linear system.
solution: Using $14\alpha^2=31\alpha-3\lambda$ and $35\alpha^2=53\alpha-4\lambda$, the roots are $31u-3$ and $53u-4$, where $u=\frac\alpha\lambda$.
To find $u$, divide (i) and (ii) by $\alpha$ and put $p=\frac\lambda\alpha$: $14\alpha+3p=31$ and $35\alpha+4p=53$.
Roots: $\frac{31}7-3=\frac{10}7$ and $\frac{53}7-4=\frac{25}7$; sum $5$, product $\frac{250}{49}$, so $49x^2-245x+250=0$: option (A).

useful_results: Common root of $a_1x^2+b_1x+c_1$ and $a_2x^2+b_2x+c_2$: $x=\frac{a_2c_1-a_1c_2}{a_1b_2-a_2b_1}$. Here it gives $\alpha=\frac\lambda7$.
Condition for a common root: $(a_1c_2-a_2c_1)^2=(a_1b_2-a_2b_1)(b_1c_2-b_2c_1)$ (check: $x^2-3x+2$ and $x^2-5x+4$ share $x=1$ and give $4=4$).
Ratios like $\frac\alpha\beta$ are best rewritten as $\frac{\alpha^2}{\alpha\beta}$ so that $p(\alpha)=0$ and the product of roots can be used.

concepts: Radical equations: domain, squaring and extraneous roots
questions.question: The number of real roots of the equation $\sqrt{x^2-4x+3}+\sqrt{x^2-9}=\sqrt{4x^2-14x+6}$ is:
questions.key_idea: All three radicands share the factor $x-3$, so $x=3$ is a root; elsewhere compare after dividing out $\sqrt{|x-3|}$.
solution: Domain: the three radicands are $\ge0$ together only for $x\le-3$ or $x\ge3$.
$x=3$: every radical is $0$, so $0+0=0$ holds and $x=3$ is a root.
$\frac76$ is not in $x>3$ (and $x-2<0$ makes (2) impossible), so it is rejected.
Case $x\le-3$: divide by $\sqrt{3-x}$: $\sqrt{1-x}+\sqrt{-3-x}=\sqrt{2-4x}$; squaring gives $\sqrt{x^2+2x-3}=2-x$, and squaring again gives $x=\frac76$, which is not $\le-3$: rejected.
The only real root is $x=3$: number of real roots $=1$: option (C).
questions.correction_note: The PDF divides by $\sqrt{x-3}$ and treats only the case $x>3$; it never considers the other part of the domain, $x\le-3$ (where $\sqrt{(x-1)(x-3)}=\sqrt{1-x}\sqrt{3-x}$ etc.). Added that branch (it also gives only $x=\frac76$, rejected). Final answer 1 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Do not solve: compare the two sides with one squaring and the sign of $6x-7$.
solution: Domain is $x\le-3$ or $x\ge3$; $x=3$ gives $0+0=0$, a root.
For $x>3$ divide by $\sqrt{x-3}$ and compare $L=\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{x+3}$ with $R=\sqrt{4x-2}$ (both positive).
Since $x^2+2x-3-(x-2)^2=6x-7>0$ and $x-2>0$, $\sqrt{x^2+2x-3}>x-2$, so $L>R$ for every $x>3$: no root there.
So the only root is $x=3$: exactly $1$ real root: option (C).

useful_results: For $\sqrt A+\sqrt B=\sqrt C$ state the domain first; a common factor such as $\sqrt{x-3}$ may be divided out only where it is non-zero, and the point where it vanishes must be tested separately.
Squaring can create extraneous roots; always test the survivors in the original equation (here $x=\frac76$ fails).
Factorise radicands before squaring: $4x^2-14x+6=2(2x-1)(x-3)$ shares $x-3$ with the other two, which is the hint that $x=3$ is special.
Sign test instead of solving: $\sqrt{u}>v\iff u>v^2$ when $v\ge0$; here the sign of $6x-7$ decides the comparison on each branch.

concepts: Quartic reducible by $t-\frac1t=z$ and exponential equations
questions.question: The equation $e^{4x}+8e^{3x}+13e^{2x}-8e^{x}+1=0$, $x\in\mathbb R$ has:
options: four solutions two of which are negative
two solutions and only one of them is negative
two solutions and both are negative
questions.key_idea: Coefficients $1,8,13,-8,1$: divide by $t^2$ and use $t^2+\frac1{t^2}=\left(t-\frac1t\right)^2+2$.
solution: $x=\ln\frac{\sqrt{13}-3}2$ or $x=\ln\frac{\sqrt{29}-5}2$; both $t$ values lie in $(0,1)$ ($\approx0.303$ and $0.193$), so both $x$ are negative.

alternate_solutions.idea: Factorise the quartic by the ansatz $(t^2+pt-1)(t^2+qt-1)$ and count positive roots by sign of the constant term.
solution: Match with $t^4+8t^3+13t^2-8t+1$: $p+q=8$ and $pq-2=13$, so $pq=15$ and $\{p,q\}=\{3,5\}$; the $t$-term $-(p+q)t=-8t$ matches too.
Each quadratic has product of roots $-1$, so exactly one positive and one negative root: exactly two positive $t$, hence exactly two real $x=\ln t$.
For $g(t)=t^2+3t-1$ and $h(t)=t^2+5t-1$: $g(0)=h(0)=-1<0$ and $g(1)=3>0$, $h(1)=5>0$, so each positive root lies in $(0,1)$.
Hence $t<1$ and $x=\ln t<0$ for both: two solutions, both negative: option (C).

useful_results: $t^4+pt^3+qt^2+pt+1$ (palindromic): divide by $t^2$ and use $z=t+\frac1t$; $t^4+pt^3+qt^2-pt+1$ (the sign flips): use $z=t-\frac1t$, since $t^2+\frac1{t^2}=z^2+2$.
Factorisation shortcut: $(t^2+pt-1)(t^2+qt-1)=t^4+(p+q)t^3+(pq-2)t^2-(p+q)t+1$.
$t-\frac1t$ is strictly increasing on $t>0$, so each real $z$ gives exactly one positive $t$; $z<0\iff0<t<1\iff x=\ln t<0$.
A quadratic $t^2+kt-1$ always has one positive and one negative root (product $-1$).

concepts: Range of a rational function using the discriminant
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb R-\{2,6\}\to\mathbb R$ be defined by $f(x)=\frac{x^2+2x+1}{x^2-8x+12}$. Then the range of $f$ is:
questions.key_idea: Set $y=f(x)$ and demand a real $x$; treat $y=1$ (leading coefficient $0$) separately.
solution: Case $y=1$: $x^2+2x+1=x^2-8x+12\Rightarrow10x=11\Rightarrow x=\frac{11}{10}$, an allowed point, so $y=1$ is attained.
The excluded points $x=2,6$ cause no loss: there the numerator is $9$ and $49$, not $0$, so no $y$ depends on them.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use calculus on each branch of the domain: turning points, limits and continuity.
solution: $f'(x)=\frac{2(x+1)(16-5x)}{(x^2-8x+12)^2}$, so the critical points are $x=-1$ and $x=\frac{16}5$.
On $(2,6)$ the denominator is negative, so $f<0$; $f\to-\infty$ at both ends and the only turning point is the maximum $-\frac{21}4$: range $\left(-\infty,-\frac{21}4\right]$.
On $(-\infty,2)$: $f\to1^-$ at $-\infty$, falls to $f(-1)=0$ (minimum, since the numerator is a square), then rises to $+\infty$ as $x\to2^-$: range $[0,\infty)$ by continuity.

useful_results: Range of $\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$: put $y=f(x)$, get a quadratic in $x$, require $D\ge0$; when the $x^2$ coefficient vanishes for some $y$ (here $y=1$) test that case separately.
Check the excluded domain points: a value $y$ is lost only if its sole preimage is an excluded $x$ (impossible here since the numerator is non-zero at $2$ and $6$).
Turning points via $f'=0$: $f'(x)=\frac{2(x+1)(16-5x)}{(x^2-8x+12)^2}$ gives $f(-1)=0$ and $f\left(\frac{16}5\right)=-\frac{21}4$.
Same-degree rational functions tend to the ratio of leading coefficients ($1$ here) at $\pm\infty$.

concepts: Location of roots of a quadratic (sign of $f$ at given points)
questions.question: The number of integral values of $k$ for which one root of the equation $2x^2-8x+k=0$ lies in the interval $(1,2)$ and its other root lies in the interval $(2,3)$ is:
questions.key_idea: With positive leading coefficient, roots in $(1,2)$ and $(2,3)$ mean $f(1)>0$, $f(2)<0$, $f(3)>0$.
solution: Let $f(x)=2x^2-8x+k$; its leading coefficient is positive, so one root in $(1,2)$ and the other in $(2,3)$ requires $f(1)>0$, $f(2)<0$, $f(3)>0$.
Combining: $k\in(6,8)$, so the only integer is $k=7$.
Number of integral values of $k$ is $1$: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the symmetry of the parabola about its axis $x=2$: the roots are $2\pm d$.
solution: The axis of $2x^2-8x+k$ is $x=\frac{8}{4}=2$, so the roots are $2-d$ and $2+d$ with $d=\sqrt{4-\frac k2}\ge0$.
One root in $(1,2)$ means $2-d\in(1,2)$, i.e. $0<d<1$; then $2+d\in(2,3)$ automatically.
The only integer is $k=7$ (roots $2\pm\frac1{\sqrt2}$): one value, option (C).

useful_results: For $a>0$: one root in $(p,q)$ and the other in $(q,r)$ $\iff f(p)>0,\ f(q)<0,\ f(r)>0$; no discriminant is needed.
The roots of $ax^2+bx+c$ are $-\frac b{2a}\pm d$, symmetric about the axis; roots on two sides of the axis $x=2$ at distances less than $1$ means $0<d<1$.
Sign change of $f$ at the middle point guarantees exactly one root on each side (intermediate value theorem for a quadratic).

concepts: Roots of an odd polynomial equation; substitution $t=x^2$ and complex roots
questions.question: Let $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_7$ be the roots of the equation $x^7+3x^5-13x^3-15x=0$ and $|\alpha_1|\ge|\alpha_2|\ge\dots\ge|\alpha_7|$. Then $\alpha_1\alpha_2-\alpha_3\alpha_4+\alpha_5\alpha_6$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Roots come in $\pm r$ pairs, and the ordering by modulus puts each pair side by side.
useful_results: An odd polynomial $x\,g(x^2)$ has roots $0$ and the pairs $\pm\sqrt{t_i}$ where $g(t_i)=0$; the product of a pair $\pm r$ is $-r^2$.
For equal-modulus ties the order inside a pair does not matter here, because the products $\alpha_1\alpha_2$, etc. are products of whole $\pm$ pairs.
Rational-root test on $t^3+3t^2-13t-15$ (divisors of $15$): $t=3$ works, then factor the quadratic $t^2+6t+5$.
Here the pair products are $-t$ for $t=-5,3,-1$, i.e. $5,-3,1$.

concepts: Power sums of roots from $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$; product of values of a parameter
questions.question: Let $a\in\mathbb R$ and let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2+60^{1/4}x+a=0$. If $\alpha^4+\beta^4=-30$, then the product of all possible values of $a$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: Write $\alpha^4+\beta^4$ in terms of $s=\alpha+\beta$ and $p=\alpha\beta=a$ to get a quadratic in $a$, whose product of roots is read off.
solution: Its discriminant is $240-180=60>0$, so both values of $a$ are real (they are $\sqrt{15}$ and $3\sqrt{15}$).
Product of the possible values of $a$ $=45$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Centre the roots at their mean, $m\pm w$, so that odd powers of $w$ cancel.
solution: Its roots are real ($D=60>0$) and their product is $45$.

useful_results: With $s=\alpha+\beta$, $p=\alpha\beta$: $\alpha^2+\beta^2=s^2-2p$, $\alpha^3+\beta^3=s^3-3sp$, $\alpha^4+\beta^4=s^4-4s^2p+2p^2$, $\alpha^5+\beta^5=s^5-5s^3p+5sp^2$ (check with $1,2$: $17$ and $33$).

When the unknown parameter is $p$ itself, the condition becomes a quadratic in $p$ and the product (or sum) of its admissible values follows from Vieta without solving, provided the roots are admissible (here real).
Centring the roots as $m\pm w$ is a quick way to expand even powers.

concepts: Common root of two quadratics
questions.question: If the value of the real number $a>0$ for which $x^2-5ax+1=0$ and $x^2-ax-5=0$ have a common real root is $\frac3{\sqrt{2\beta}}$, then $\beta$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: A common root satisfies a linear combination of the two equations, which fixes it in terms of $a$.
solution: Let $\alpha$ be the common root: $\alpha^2-5a\alpha+1=0$ and $\alpha^2-a\alpha-5=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Subtract the two equations to get a linear equation for the common root, then substitute back.
solution: A common root satisfies the difference: $(x^2-5ax+1)-(x^2-ax-5)=-4ax+6=0$, so $\alpha=\frac3{2a}$.

useful_results: For $x^2+p_1x+q_1$ and $x^2+p_2x+q_2$ the common root is $x=\frac{q_2-q_1}{p_1-p_2}$ (from the difference of the equations).
A common root exists iff $(q_2-q_1)^2=(p_2-p_1)(p_1q_2-p_2q_1)$. Here it gives $36=4a\cdot26a$, so $a^2=\frac9{26}$.
Subtracting equations is faster than cross-multiplication whenever the $x^2$ coefficients are equal.

concepts: Equations with modulus of a quadratic expression
questions.question: The sum of all the roots of the equation $\left|x^2-8x+15\right|-2x+7=0$ is:
questions.key_idea: Split at the roots $3,5$ of the quadratic inside the modulus and check each candidate against its interval.
solution: Case I: $x\in(-\infty,3]\cup[5,\infty)$, where the quadratic is $\ge0$: $x^2-8x+15-2x+7=0$.
$5+\sqrt3\approx6.73\ge5$ is accepted; $5-\sqrt3\approx3.27$ lies in $(3,5)$, so it is rejected in this case.
Case II: $x\in(3,5)$, where the quadratic is negative: $-x^2+8x-15-2x+7=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Isolate the modulus: it equals $2x-7$, which forces $x\ge\frac72$; then square and factor a difference of squares.
solution: Keep only $x\ge\frac72$: $5+\sqrt3\approx6.73$ and $4$ qualify; $5-\sqrt3\approx3.27$ and $2$ do not.

useful_results: $|f(x)|=g(x)$ forces $g(x)\ge0$ first; then $f=\pm g$, or square and use $f^2-g^2=(f-g)(f+g)$.
For $|(x-p)(x-q)|$ the quadratic is negative strictly between $p$ and $q$; split the line there.
Always test each candidate against its case interval or the side condition $g\ge0$ (here $5-\sqrt3$ and $2$ fail).

concepts: Relations between roots and coefficients of a cubic; cube roots of unity
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the three roots of the equation $x^3+bx+c=0$. If $\beta\gamma=1=-\alpha$, then $b^3+2c^3-3\alpha^3-6\beta^3-8\gamma^3$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: From $\alpha=-1$, the sum $0$ and $\beta\gamma=1$ fix $b$ and $c$; then $x^3=-1$ gives every cube.

alternate_solutions.idea: With $b=0$ the cubic is $x^3+c=0$, so all three roots have the same cube.
solution: With $b=0$, $c=1$ the equation is $x^3+1=0$, so every root satisfies $x^3=-1$: $\alpha^3=\beta^3=\gamma^3=-1$.
(The roots are $-1,\,e^{\pm i\pi/3}$; they have sum $0$ and $\beta\gamma=1$, as required.)

useful_results: For $x^3+bx+c=0$ each root satisfies $r^3=-br-c$; so $\sum r^3=-3c$ and if $b=0$ all roots have the same cube $-c$.
$1+\omega+\omega^2=0$ and $\omega^3=1$; the roots of $x^2-x+1=0$ are $-\omega,-\omega^2$.
Vieta with one known root: use the sum to get $\beta+\gamma$, the product to get $\beta\gamma$ and the pair sum for $b$.

concepts: Complex roots of a real quadratic in polar form and power sums $\alpha^n+\beta^n$
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the quadratic equation $x^2+\sqrt6x+3=0$. Then $\frac{\alpha^{23}+\beta^{23}+\alpha^{14}+\beta^{14}}{\alpha^{15}+\beta^{15}+\alpha^{10}+\beta^{10}}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The roots are $\sqrt3e^{\pm3\pi i/4}$, so $\alpha^n+\beta^n=2\cdot3^{n/2}\cos\frac{3n\pi}4$ and the $\cos$ factors cancel or vanish.
solution: Roots: $x=\frac{-\sqrt6\pm\sqrt{-6}}2=\sqrt6\cdot\frac{-1\pm i}2=\sqrt3\cdot\frac{-1\pm i}{\sqrt2}$, so $\alpha=\sqrt3e^{3\pi i/4}$ and $\beta=\sqrt3e^{-3\pi i/4}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working stops after writing $\alpha=\sqrt3e^{i3\pi/4}$ and gives no further steps, and its printed key is (D) 9, which is wrong. The exact value is 81 (checked numerically to 12 digits), option (B). Solution written from that point.

alternate_solutions.idea: Algebraic route without trigonometry: $a_2=0$ forces $\alpha^4=\beta^4=-9$, so $a_{n+4}=-9a_n$.

useful_results: Complex conjugate roots $re^{\pm i\theta}$: $\alpha^n+\beta^n=2r^n\cos n\theta$ and $\alpha\beta=r^2$. For $x^2+px+q$ with $p^2<4q$: $r=\sqrt q$ and $\cos\theta=-\frac p{2\sqrt q}$.
If $a_2=\alpha^2+\beta^2=0$ (that is $p^2=2q$), then $\alpha^4=\beta^4=-q^2$ and $a_{n+4}=-q^2a_n$; for $x^2+\sqrt6x+3$ this is $a_{n+4}=-9a_n$.
Never trust a printed key blindly: recompute the ratio numerically; here it is exactly $81$, option (B), not $9$.

concepts: Modular inequality $|f(n)|<c$ with a quadratic, counted over integers
questions.question: The number of elements in the set $\left\{n\in\mathbb Z:\left|n^2-10n+19\right|<6\right\}$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: $|g|<6$ splits into $g>-6$ and $g<6$; the first is a perfect square and excludes only $n=5$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the bounds of (ii) as $5-3\sqrt2<n<5+3\sqrt2$, but the roots of $n^2-10n+13$ are $5\pm2\sqrt3$ (discriminant 48). Its list from (i) $\cap$ (ii) is also written as $\{2,3,4,5,6,8\}$, which wrongly keeps 5 and drops 7; the correct set is $\{2,3,4,6,7,8\}$. The count 6 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Complete the square, $n^2-10n+19=(n-5)^2-6$, and count integers $m=n-5$.

useful_results: Complete the square first: $n^2-10n+19=(n-5)^2-6$; then $|(n-5)^2-6|<6\iff0<(n-5)^2<12$.
Counting integers with $m^2<c$: $|m|\le\lceil\sqrt c\,\rceil-1$ (here $|m|\le3$ since $9<12\le16$).
A strict lower bound that is a perfect square, such as $(n-5)^2>0$, removes exactly the single point $n=5$.

concepts: Power sums $a^n+b^n$ by Newton's relation and recurrence
questions.question: If $a$ and $b$ are the roots of the equation $x^2-7x-1=0$, then the value of $\frac{a^{21}+b^{21}+a^{17}+b^{17}}{a^{19}+b^{19}}$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Use $S_{n+2}=7S_{n+1}+S_n$ to eliminate $S_{17},S_{18},S_{20},S_{21}$ in favour of $S_{19}$.
solution: $a^2=7a+1$ and $b^2=7b+1$, so by Newton's theorem $S_{n+2}-7S_{n+1}-S_n=0$ where $S_n=a^n+b^n$.
From the first: $S_{21}-7S_{20}=S_{19}$, so the numerator is $51S_{19}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $ab=-1$, $\frac1{a^2}=b^2$, so the numerator factors as $(a^2+b^2)(a^{19}+b^{19})$.
solution: Adding: numerator $=(a^2+b^2)(a^{19}+b^{19})$, so the ratio equals $a^2+b^2$.

useful_results: If $ab=1$ the same gives $S_{n+2}+S_{n-2}=\left(S_1^2-2\right)S_n$.
Newton's recurrence: for $x^2=px+q$, $S_{n+2}=pS_{n+1}+qS_n$; here $p=7$, $q=1$.

concepts: Recurrence satisfied by $A\alpha^n+B\beta^n$ (Newton's relation)
questions.question: If $\alpha,\beta$ are the roots of the equation $x^2-x-1=0$ and $S_n=2023\alpha^n+2024\beta^n$, then:
questions.key_idea: Each of $\alpha,\beta$ satisfies $x^2=x+1$, so any combination $A\alpha^n+B\beta^n$ obeys $S_{n+2}=S_{n+1}+S_n$.
solution: Multiply by $2023$ and $2024$ and add: $S_{n+2}=S_{n+1}+S_n$, i.e. $S_n-S_{n-1}-S_{n-2}=0$ (Newton's method).
useful_results: If $\alpha,\beta$ are roots of $x^2=px+q$ then every sequence $S_n=A\alpha^n+B\beta^n$ (any constants $A,B$) satisfies $S_{n+2}=pS_{n+1}+qS_n$.
For $x^2-x-1=0$ this is the Fibonacci recurrence; $\alpha^n+\beta^n$ gives the Lucas numbers $2,1,3,4,7,11,\dots$.
The constants $2023,2024$ are a distraction: only the quadratic decides the recurrence.

concepts: Quadratic expression of constant sign (conditions on $a$ and $D$)
questions.question: Let $S$ be the set of positive integral values of $a$ for which $\frac{ax^2+2(a+1)x+9a+4}{x^2-8x+32}<0$, $\forall x\in\mathbb R$. Then the number of elements in $S$ is:
questions.key_idea: The denominator is always positive, so the numerator must be negative for all $x$, forcing $a<0$.
solution: Denominator: $x^2-8x+32=(x-4)^2+16>0$ for all real $x$, so the fraction has the sign of the numerator.
So we need $ax^2+2(a+1)x+9a+4<0$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$.
A quadratic is negative for all real $x$ only if its leading coefficient is negative: $a<0$ (and $D<0$).
But $S$ consists of positive integers $a$, which contradicts $a<0$ (for $a>0$ the numerator is positive for large $|x|$).
So $S=\varnothing$ and the number of elements is $0$: option (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF working is cut off after the single line $a<0$; it never states the denominator is positive nor concludes the count. Completed the argument; the answer (B) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Look at the fraction as $x\to\pm\infty$: it tends to $a$.
solution: If $a>0$, the fraction is close to $a>0$ for large $|x|$, so it cannot be negative for all real $x$.
So no positive $a$ works: $S=\varnothing$ and $n(S)=0$: option (B).

useful_results: $ax^2+bx+c<0$ for all real $x$ $\iff a<0$ and $D<0$; if $a>0$ the quadratic is positive for large $|x|$.
First check the sign of a quadratic denominator ($D<0$ and positive leading coefficient means it is always positive); then the sign of the fraction is the sign of the numerator.
For $\frac{N(x)}{D(x)}$ of equal degrees the limit at $\pm\infty$ is the ratio of leading coefficients, which must be $\le0$ if the fraction is negative everywhere.

concepts: Exponential equation with conjugate surds, $u^x+u^{-x}=c$
questions.question: Let $S=\left\{x\in\mathbb R:\left(\sqrt3+\sqrt2\right)^x+\left(\sqrt3-\sqrt2\right)^x=10\right\}$. Then the number of elements in $S$ is:
questions.key_idea: $(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)=1$, so the equation is $t+\frac1t=10$ with $t=(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Recognise $2\cosh$: the equation is $\cosh(\lambda x)=5$, an even, strictly monotone function on $x\ge0$.
solution: Let $\lambda=\ln\left(\sqrt3+\sqrt2\right)>0$. Since $\sqrt3-\sqrt2=\left(\sqrt3+\sqrt2\right)^{-1}$, the equation is $e^{\lambda x}+e^{-\lambda x}=10$, i.e. $\cosh(\lambda x)=5$.
$\cosh$ is even and strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$ from $1$ to $\infty$, so $\cosh u=5$ has exactly two solutions $u=\pm u_0$ (because $5>1$).
Hence exactly two real $x=\pm\frac{u_0}\lambda$: $2$ elements, option (D).

useful_results: For $u>0$, $u\ne1$: $u^x+u^{-x}=c$ has two solutions $\pm x_0$ if $c>2$, one ($x=0$) if $c=2$ and none if $c<2$ (AM-GM, $u^x+u^{-x}\ge2$).
Conjugate surd pairs have product $1$ here: $(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^2=5+2\sqrt6$, so $(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^{2}+(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)^2=10$.
$u^x+u^{-x}=c$ reduces to $t^2-ct+1=0$ whose two roots are reciprocals.

concepts: Natural-number roots from $\alpha+\beta=70$ and divisibility of the product
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N$ be roots of the equation $x^2-70x+\lambda=0$, where $\frac\lambda2,\frac\lambda3\notin\mathbb N$. If $\lambda$ assumes the minimum possible value, then $\frac{\left(\sqrt{\alpha-1}+\sqrt{\beta-1}\right)(\lambda+35)}{|\alpha-\beta|}$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $\alpha+\beta=70$ fixed, so $\lambda=\alpha\beta$ is smallest for the smallest admissible $\alpha$, subject to $2\nmid\lambda$, $3\nmid\lambda$.
solution:
So $\lambda=\alpha(70-\alpha)$. The condition $ rac\lambda2, rac\lambda3
otin\mathbb N$ means $2
mid\lambda$ and $3
mid\lambda$.

$\lambda$ increases with $\alpha$ for $\alpha<35$, so try $\alpha=1,2,3,\dots$: $\alpha=1$: $\lambda=69$, divisible by $3$; $\alpha=2$: $\lambda=136$, even; $\alpha=3$: $\lambda=201$, divisible by $3$; $\alpha=4$: $\lambda=264$, even.
$\alpha=5$: $\lambda=5\cdot65=325$, which is odd and not divisible by $3$: admissible.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's first line writes the equation as $x^2-7x+\lambda=0$ (typo for $70x$; it then correctly uses $\alpha+\beta=70$), and it jumps to $\alpha=5,\beta=65,\lambda=325$ without showing why smaller $\alpha$ fail. Fixed the typo and added the check of $\alpha=1,\dots,4$. The answer 60 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use residues mod $6$: both roots must be coprime to $6$, which forces $\alpha\equiv\beta\equiv5\pmod6$.
solution: $2\nmid\lambda$ and $3\nmid\lambda$ with $\lambda=\alpha\beta$ mean neither $\alpha$ nor $\beta$ is divisible by $2$ or $3$, i.e. $\alpha,\beta\equiv\pm1\pmod6$.
$\alpha+\beta=70\equiv4\pmod6$; the possible sums of residues $\pm1,\pm1$ are $2,0,-2\equiv4$, so both must be $\equiv-1\equiv5\pmod6$.

useful_results: For a fixed sum $S=\alpha+\beta$, the product $\alpha(S-\alpha)=\frac{S^2}4-\left(\frac S2-\alpha\right)^2$ increases as $\alpha$ moves towards $\frac S2$; the minimum product uses the smallest admissible $\alpha$.
A product is coprime to $6$ iff each factor is; both roots then are $\pm1\pmod6$, and the sum $70\equiv4\pmod6$ forces both to be $5\pmod6$.
Integer roots of $x^2-Sx+\lambda$ correspond to factor pairs $(\alpha,S-\alpha)$; list from the extreme to cut down the search.

concepts: Range (maximum and minimum) of a rational function by the discriminant method
questions.question: Let the sum of the maximum and the minimum values of the function $f(x)=\frac{2x^2-3x+8}{2x^2+3x+8}$ be $\frac mn$, where $\gcd(m,n)=1$. Then $m+n$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Put $y=f(x)$ and require real $x$; the extreme values are the roots of the resulting discriminant condition.
solution: Let $f(x)=\frac{2x^2-3x+8}{2x^2+3x+8}=y$. The denominator $2x^2+3x+8>0$ for all real $x$ (its discriminant is $9-64<0$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's second line of the discriminant condition reads $9(y+1)^2-64y(y-1)^2\ge0$, with a stray factor $y$ (and a wrong power); the correct expression is $9(y+1)^2-64(y-1)^2\ge0$, which is what the next line actually uses. Fixed; answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Divide by $x$ and put $w=2x+\frac8x$; then $f=\frac{w-3}{w+3}$ and AM-GM bounds $w$.
solution: For $x\ne0$, divide numerator and denominator by $x$: with $w=2x+\frac8x$, $f=\frac{w-3}{w+3}=1-\frac6{w+3}$.
On $w\ge8$, $f$ increases from $f(8)=\frac5{11}$ towards $1$; on $w\le-8$, $f$ increases from $1$ (as $w\to-\infty$) to $f(-8)=\frac{-11}{-5}=\frac{11}5$. Also $f(0)=1$.
So the range is $\left[\frac5{11},\frac{11}5\right]$: minimum at $x=2$, maximum at $x=-2$.

useful_results: For $\frac{ax^2-bx+c}{ax^2+bx+c}$ divide by $x$: with $w=ax+\frac cx$ ($|w|\ge2\sqrt{ac}$ for real $x\neq0$) it becomes $\frac{w-b}{w+b}$.
In the discriminant method the extreme values are the roots of the discriminant quadratic: here $55y^2-146y+55\le0$, so max $+$ min $=\frac{146}{55}$ (sum of roots) and max $\times$ min $=1$.
Check: $f(2)=\frac5{11}$ and $f(-2)=\frac{11}5$.

concepts: Formation of a quadratic with given roots; Vieta's relations
questions.question: If $2$ and $6$ are the roots of the equation $ax^2+bx+1=0$, then the quadratic equation whose roots are $\frac1{2a+b}$ and $\frac1{6a+b}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Vieta on $2,6$ gives $a=\frac1{12}$ and $b=-\frac23$, from which $2a+b$ and $6a+b$ are numbers.

alternate_solutions.idea: Read $2a+b$ and $6a+b$ as the derivative $f'(1)$ and $f'(3)$ of $f(x)=ax^2+bx+1$.

useful_results: $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ has $f'(x)=2ax+b$, so $ka+b=f'\left(\frac k2\right)$: expressions such as $2a+b$, $6a+b$ are slopes at $x=1,3$.
If $f$ has roots $r_1,r_2$ and $f(0)=c$, then $f(x)=\frac{c}{r_1r_2}(x-r_1)(x-r_2)$.
A quadratic with roots $u,v$: $x^2-(u+v)x+uv=0$; here $u=-2$, $v=-6$.

concepts: Newton's relation for power sums and minimum value of a quadratic
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the distinct roots of the equation $x^2-\left(t^2-5t+6\right)x+1=0$, $t\in\mathbb R$ and $a_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$. Then the minimum value of $\frac{a_{2023}+a_{2025}}{a_{2024}}$ is:
questions.key_idea: With $\alpha\beta=1$, $a_{n+2}+a_n=(\alpha+\beta)a_{n+1}$, so the ratio is just $t^2-5t+6$.
solution: The minimum of $t^2-5t+6$ is $-\frac D{4a}=-\frac{25-24}4=-\frac14$, at $t=\frac52$.

At $t=\frac52$ the sum is $-\frac14$, so $|\alpha+\beta|<2$ and the roots are distinct complex conjugates, which is allowed. With $a_n=2\cos n\theta$, $\cos\theta=-\frac18$ and $\frac\theta\pi$ irrational, $a_{2024}\ne0$.
useful_results: If $\alpha\beta=1$ and $s=\alpha+\beta$, then $a_{n+2}+a_n=s\,a_{n+1}$ for every $n$, so $\frac{a_{n+2}+a_n}{a_{n+1}}=s$ regardless of $n$.
Min of $t^2-5t+6$: vertex $t=\frac52$, value $-\frac14$.
When $|s|<2$ the roots are $e^{\pm i\theta}$ with $s=2\cos\theta$, $a_n=2\cos n\theta$ and the identity is $\cos(n+2)\theta+\cos n\theta=2\cos\theta\cos(n+1)\theta$.

concepts: Power sums of roots and formation of a quadratic with new roots
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2+2\sqrt2x-1=0$. Then the quadratic equation whose roots are $\alpha^4+\beta^4$ and $\frac1{10}\left(\alpha^6+\beta^6\right)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Build $\alpha^4+\beta^4$ and $\alpha^6+\beta^6$ from $s=-2\sqrt2$ and $p=-1$ through $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ and $\alpha^3+\beta^3$.
solution: The new roots are $98$ and $97$: sum $195$, product $98\cdot97=9506$.
questions.correction_note: The last line of the PDF reads $x^2-195x+95x+9506=0$ (a stray $+95x$ term) after correctly writing $x^2-(98+97)x+(98)(97)=0$. The correct equation is $x^2-195x+9506=0$. Everything before it is right and the option (C) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the roots explicitly: $\alpha,\beta=-\sqrt2\pm\sqrt3$, so $\alpha^2,\beta^2=5\mp2\sqrt6$.

useful_results: With $s=\alpha+\beta$, $p=\alpha\beta$: $S_2=s^2-2p$, $S_3=s^3-3sp$, $S_4=S_2^2-2p^2$, $S_6=S_3^2-2p^3=S_2\left(S_4-p^2\right)$.
When the discriminant is $4\times$ a non-square, solve explicitly: roots $-\sqrt2\pm\sqrt3$ have squares $5\mp2\sqrt6$ (conjugate surds, product $1$).
A quadratic with roots $u,v$ is $x^2-(u+v)x+uv=0$.

concepts: Newton's relation for $\alpha^n-\beta^n$ and reduction of a linear recurrence expression
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta$; $\alpha>\beta$, be the roots of the equation $x^2-\sqrt2x-\sqrt3=0$. Let $P_n=\alpha^n-\beta^n$, $n\in\mathbb N$. Then $\left(11\sqrt3-10\sqrt2\right)P_{10}+\left(11\sqrt2+10\right)P_{11}-11P_{12}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $P_n=\alpha^n-\beta^n$ obeys $P_{n+2}=\sqrt2P_{n+1}+\sqrt3P_n$; use it to push $P_{12},P_{11}$ down to $P_9,P_{10}$.
solution: Let $E$ be the expression. Substitute $P_{12}$ and $P_{11}$ (second term): $E=\left(11\sqrt3-10\sqrt2\right)P_{10}+\left(11\sqrt2+10\right)\left(\sqrt2P_{10}+\sqrt3P_9\right)-11\left(\sqrt2P_{11}+\sqrt3P_{10}\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the identity on a single root: reduce $g(x)=\left(11\sqrt3-10\sqrt2\right)x+\left(11\sqrt2+10\right)x^2-11x^3$ modulo $x^2-\sqrt2x-\sqrt3$.
solution: $E=\alpha^9g(\alpha)-\beta^9g(\beta)$ with $g(x)=\left(11\sqrt3-10\sqrt2\right)x+\left(11\sqrt2+10\right)x^2-11x^3$, so it is enough to simplify $g$ at a root.

useful_results: The difference sequence $P_n=\alpha^n-\beta^n$ satisfies the same recurrence as $\alpha^n+\beta^n$: $P_{n+2}=sP_{n+1}-pP_n$ (here $s=\sqrt2$, $p=-\sqrt3$).
A combination $\sum c_kP_{n+k}$ equals $\alpha^n g(\alpha)-\beta^n g(\beta)$ with $g(x)=\sum c_kx^k$; reducing $g$ modulo the quadratic gives the answer for all $n$ at once.
Substituting only the highest index first: $E=10\left(P_{11}-\sqrt2P_{10}\right)=10\sqrt3P_9$.

concepts: Power sums $U_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$ and the relation $x^2+\sqrt2x=8$
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be roots of $x^2+\sqrt2x-8=0$. If $U_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$, then $\frac{U_{10}+\sqrt2U_9}{2U_8}$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Each root satisfies $x+\sqrt2=\frac8x$, so $x^9(x+\sqrt2)=8x^8$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $\alpha+\beta=\sqrt2$; for $x^2+\sqrt2x-8=0$ the sum of the roots is $-\sqrt2$ (the sign of $\alpha\beta=-8$ is right). The wrong sign is not used later, so the answer 4 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use Newton's recurrence directly: $U_{n+2}=-\sqrt2U_{n+1}+8U_n$.

useful_results: For $x^2+px+q=0$ the power sums obey $U_{n+2}=-pU_{n+1}-qU_n$, so $\frac{U_{n+2}+pU_{n+1}}{U_n}=-q$ whenever $U_n\ne0$. Here $p=\sqrt2$, $q=-8$: the ratio is $\frac{8}{2}=4$ after dividing by $2$.
Each root satisfies $x+p=-\frac qx$; this converts $x^{n+1}(x+p)$ into $-q\,x^n$.
For real roots, even power sums are positive, so dividing by $U_8$ is safe.
